lesson.title: GPS and Relativity Investigation
lesson.buzzAssessmentTitle: Unit 5 Honors: GPS and Relativity Investigation

assessmentSettings.feedbackPolicy: Show concise learning feedback after submission; keep full answer keys in the teacher setup file.

requiredCopiedValues: Students read values from the on-screen evidence tables while answering the native Buzz questions.
evidenceRequirements.missingEvidenceAction: Use the on-screen evidence table and route contradictory or unverifiable written responses to human review.

humanReviewTriggers: Student response conflicts with the on-screen evidence table.
Student reports values that fall outside the expected range but the recorded evidence may support them.
Student gives a partially correct explanation that does not fit the rubric cleanly.
Student uses valid alternative vocabulary or reasoning not covered by the model answer.
Student answer is blank, copied from the prompt, or too vague to verify.
Student cites no data when the prompt requires their own recorded values.

questions.prompt: Describe both relativistic effects acting on the satellite clock. For each, state what causes it and which direction it pushes the clock. Use all three of your Part B values as evidence, and say which effect wins.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on naming the cause and direction of each effect and on using all three of your Part B values as evidence.

criteria: States that the satellite sits higher in Earth's gravitational field so its clock gains time, and that it moves rapidly in orbit so its clock loses time; quotes all three recorded values including their signs; identifies the gravity effect as the larger one; and shows that the two individual values combine to give the recorded net value.
Names both effects with the correct directions and quotes some values, but does not show how the two combine into the net result or omits one of the three values.
Reverses the direction of either effect, treats only one effect as real, or cites no recorded values.

commonMisconceptions: Reverses which effect speeds the clock up and which slows it down.
Treats the two effects as cancelling exactly at GPS altitude.
Reports the net value without showing it comes from the two separate terms.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your answer uses recorded evidence and connects it to the correct physics idea.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by adding the specific recorded values and completing the physics reasoning requested in the prompt.
feedback.noCredit: Return to the on-screen evidence, identify the values this question asks about, and explain them using the target concept.
feedback.teacherNote: Flag for review if the reasoning is unusual but could be correct, or if cited values disagree with the on-screen evidence.

questions.prompt: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning conclusion defending the pre-launch GPS clock correction. Quote your Part C offset, explain what it does to the oscillator, compare the corrected and uncorrected Part D position errors, and use the time-to-failure value to show why the correction is required.
questions.gradedOn: Your response is graded on the calibration value, the physical mechanism, both mission results, and a conclusion supported by the time-to-failure evidence.
questions.requiredEvidence: part c calibration and part d mission

criteria: Quotes the recorded offset and explains that the oscillator is set slightly slow before launch so the net orbital effect speeds it to the intended received frequency; compares both one-day position errors; states that the uncorrected error accumulates continuously; cites the recorded time at which it first exceeded 10 m; and concludes that relativity is a required engineering input.
Describes the correction and gives some Part C or Part D evidence but omits the mechanism, one comparison, or the time-to-failure.
Reverses the correction, claims the error self-corrects, or gives no usable investigation evidence.

commonMisconceptions: Describes the correction as speeding up the ground oscillator.
Claims the receiver can ignore a satellite clock error because several satellites are used.
Treats the uncorrected position error as constant rather than accumulating.
Omits the measured time at which the 10 m navigation limit was exceeded.

feedback.fullCredit: Strong work. Your answer uses recorded evidence and connects it to the correct physics idea.
feedback.partialCredit: Revise by adding the specific recorded values and completing the physics reasoning requested in the prompt.
feedback.noCredit: Return to the on-screen evidence, identify the values this question asks about, and explain them using the target concept.
